analysis.one_liner: Bars members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading stocks and other securities.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban stock ownership by members of Congress and their spouses never received a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, or any other security, including hedge fund and derivative interests. Current members would have had 180 days to sell their holdings, with a $50,000 fine for each violation; diversified index-style funds, government retirement plans, and Treasury bonds would have remained allowed. It was referred to four House committees and no committee ever acted on it, so it never received a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The public benefits from removing a specific conflict: lawmakers currently write laws and sit on committees overseeing industries whose stocks they and their spouses can freely buy and sell. Banning that trading removes both the temptation and the appearance of members profiting from advance knowledge of legislation. Members themselves would bear the cost of restructuring their family finances around permitted investments.

how_it_helps.text: Members of Congress and their spouses would be barred from owning or trading stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, or any other security, removing the ability to personally profit from legislative knowledge.
Current members would have to divest within 180 days of enactment; new members within 180 days of taking office; inherited assets must be sold within 180 days.
Violations carry a civil penalty of up to $50,000 per violation, enforceable by the Attorney General or the Special Counsel in federal court.
Members forced to sell would not owe capital gains tax on the divested property if they reinvest in permitted bonds or diversified funds within 60 days, easing the transition.

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses would pay, by divesting individual stocks, bonds, and complex investments within 180 days and forfeiting the ability to trade on legislative information. Taxpayers would bear a small cost from the tax deferral for divesting members.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: Members may keep interests in hedge funds, venture capital funds, and other privately held complex investment vehicles for up to five years before divesting, a long delay for the assets hardest to price fairly.

The exceptions are broad: members and spouses may still trade securities in the course of the spouse's primary occupation, own interests in small businesses, and hold any diversified fund that does not present a conflict of interest, so a spouse's trading could still touch companies the lawmaker oversees.

Enforcement depends on the Attorney General, the Special Counsel, and the House and Senate Ethics Committees, and the cap of $50,000 per violation is small relative to many members' wealth, which could make the fine a cost of doing business rather than a real deterrent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a direct answer to a public trust problem: lawmakers currently can trade stocks in companies their committees regulate, and this bill would end that outright, with divestment deadlines, a $50,000 fine per violation [S2][S3]. The costs are real but modest: members would have to restructure family finances, deferred divestment for hedge-fund and private-equity holdings gives wealthy members up to five extra years, and enforcement depends on the executive branch and ethics committees that have historically acted rarely. On balance the drawbacks are design imperfections, not reasons the bill failed; it died from lack of leadership action, not from an evidentiary flaw.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with a handful of bipartisan cosponsors in March 2023 and sent to four House committees; none of them acted on it, no vote was ever held, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Representative Pramila Jayapal (D-WA) introduced the bill on March 21, 2023, joined by original cosponsors from both parties, including Democrats such as Rosa DeLauro and Katie Porter and Republicans such as Matt Rosendale and Ken Buck.
The same day, it was referred to four committees: Financial Services, Agriculture, House Administration, and Ways and Means. No further action of any kind appears in the record.
The bill never received a markup, a hearing, or a floor vote in either chamber, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing it.
A companion problem the bill targeted — members trading stocks in companies their own committees regulate — therefore remained legal under the disclosure-only STOCK Act framework.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress and their spouses are better off: they retain the ability to own and trade individual stocks, including in companies affected by legislation, without any new restrictions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Sitting members of Congress and their spouses

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors from both parties.

for.name: Reps. Jake Auchincloss, Rosa DeLauro, Chuy García, Andy Kim, Jerrold Nadler, Eleanor Holmes Norton, Katie Porter, Mark Takano, Paul Tonko (Democrats) and Matt Rosendale, Ken Buck (Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill its stated bipartisan character (29 total cosponsors, 21 Democrats and 8 Republicans).

against.name: House committee chairs (Financial Services, Agriculture, House Administration, Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs of the four committees of referral
against.what_they_did: None of the four committees that received the bill took any action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support leaned Democratic (21 of 29 cosponsors) but included 8 Republicans, and the bill's fate was not a party-line vote — it never reached one; the decisive inaction was the four committees' refusal to act.

industries.industry: Sitting members of Congress and their households
industries.note: The people who must vote on this bill are the ones who would have to sell their securities portfolios and give up trading in companies they help regulate. That direct self-interest is the clearest explanation for why the bill stalled after introduction.

industries.industry: Wealthy members with hedge fund and venture capital stakes
industries.note: Complex private investments must be divested too, though on a five-year timeline rather than 180 days. The long runway is an acknowledgment that some members hold substantial illiquid positions.

industries.industry: Federal ethics enforcement bodies (Attorney General, Office of Special Counsel, congressional Ethics Committees)
industries.note: The bill would give these bodies new authority to bring civil actions against members and to issue interpretive guidance, modestly expanding the machinery that polices official conduct.
